The arrangement is **three** lenses in contact: two plano-convex lenses of glass with a
**liquid lens** trapped between their curved faces.
**Step 1 — find the focal length of each glass lens.** For a plano-convex lens with the
curved face of radius 12 cm:
1/f = (n − 1)(1/R₁ − 1/R₂)
= (1·5 − 1)(1/12 − 1/∞)
= 0·5/12
**f = 24 cm** each ✓
**Step 2 — identify the liquid lens.** The liquid fills the space between the two
**convex** faces, so it takes the shape of a **biconcave** lens with
R₁ = **−12 cm**, R₂ = **+12 cm** ✓
**Step 3 — write its focal length.**
1/f_L = (n_L − 1)(−1/12 − 1/12)
= **−(n_L − 1)/6**
**Step 4 — combine all three in contact.**
1/F = 1/24 + 1/f_L + 1/24
−1/60 = 1/12 − (n_L − 1)/6
**Step 5 — solve.**
(n_L − 1)/6 = 1/12 + 1/60
= (5 + 1)/60
= 1/10
n_L − 1 = 0·6
**n_L = 1·60** ✓
**Why the combination is diverging.** The given F = **−60 cm** is negative, so the liquid
lens must be strongly **diverging** - strong enough to overcome the two converging glass
lenses ✓ That requires the liquid to be **denser** optically than the glass, and 1·60
against 1·50 is exactly that.
**A check by substitution.** With n_L = 1·6:
1/f_L = −0·6/6 = **−1/10**, so f_L = −10 cm
1/F = 1/24 − 1/10 + 1/24 = 1/12 − 1/10 = (5 − 6)/60 = **−1/60** ✓ F = −60 cm, as given.
**Why the radii take opposite signs for the liquid.** Its first surface bulges **away**
from the incoming light, the second **towards** it ✓ Getting that sign pair right is the
whole of the geometry here; treating the liquid as biconvex would give n_L < 1·5 and one
of the distractors.
**Reading the distractors.** **1·33** ✗ is water, which being less dense than glass
would make the liquid lens too weak and leave the combination converging. **1·42** ✗ and
**1·53** ✗ likewise give F values far from −60 cm ✓ Substituting each back into the
combination formula tests them in one line.
∴ 1·60.

The figure shows the **reflected** and **refracted** rays at right angles, which fixes a
relation between the angle of incidence and the two indices.
**Step 1 — use the geometry.** The reflected ray leaves at angle i on the other side of
the normal, and the refracted ray goes into the second medium at angle r. The figure
shows 90° between them, so measuring round from the surface:
i + 90° + r = 180°
**r = 90° − i** ✓
**Step 2 — apply Snell's law.**
μ₁ sin i = μ₂ sin r
= μ₂ sin(90° − i)
= **μ₂ cos i**
**Step 3 — divide by cos i.**
**tan i = μ₂/μ₁**
**Step 4 — convert to sin i.** From tan i = μ₂/μ₁ the right triangle has opposite μ₂,
adjacent μ₁ and hypotenuse √(μ₁² + μ₂²), so
**sin i = μ₂/(μ₁² + μ₂²)^(1/2)** ✓
**What this angle is called.** It is **Brewster's angle** ✓ At it the reflected light is
**completely plane-polarised**, with its electric field perpendicular to the plane of
incidence - which is why polarising sunglasses cut glare from water and roads so
effectively.
**A worked value.** For air to glass, μ₁ = 1 and μ₂ = 1·5:
tan i = 1·5, so **i = 56·3°** ✓
and then r = 90 − 56·3 = **33·7°**, which satisfies sin 56·3 = 1·5 sin 33·7, that is
0·832 = 1·5(0·555) ✓ exactly.
**Why the reflected ray is polarised there.** The refracted ray travels along the
direction in which the oscillating electrons in the medium would have to radiate to
produce the reflected ray ✓ A dipole cannot radiate along its own axis, so that
polarisation component is missing from the reflection.
**Reading the distractors.** **tan i = μ₁/μ₂** ✗ inverts the ratio - for air to glass it
would give i = 33·7°, the refraction angle rather than the incidence angle.
**sin i = μ₁μ₂** ✗ and **sin i = μ₂/μ₁** ✗ can exceed 1 and so are impossible as sines ✓
That observation eliminates both at a glance.
∴ sin i = μ₂/(μ₁² + μ₂²)^(1/2).

Light escapes only within a cone set by the **critical angle**, so the disc must cover
the circle where that cone meets the surface.
**Step 1 — find the critical angle.**
sin C = 1/n
= 1/(5/3)
= **3/5 = 0·6**
so **C = 36·9°** ✓
**Step 2 — find the tangent of that angle.** With sin C = 3/5, the right triangle has
sides 3, 4, 5, so
**tan C = 3/4**
**Step 3 — find the radius of the escape circle.** Rays leaving the source at angles
beyond C are totally internally reflected and never reach the air ✓ Only those within
the cone of half-angle C emerge, and they strike the surface inside a circle of radius
r = h tan C
= 4 x (3/4)
= **3 m** ✓
**Step 4 — conclude.** A disc of radius **3 m** centred above the source blocks every ray
that could escape ✓
**Why nothing escapes beyond the circle.** At the surface, a ray arriving at an angle
greater than C undergoes **total internal reflection** - it is turned back into the
water entirely, with no refracted part at all ✓ So the disc need only cover the circle,
not the whole pond.
**The everyday version of this.** A fish looking up sees the entire sky compressed into
a circular window of half-angle 48·8° for water - **Snell's window** ✓ Outside that
circle it sees only the reflected pond bottom. The present question is the same geometry
seen from above.
**Why the answer scales with depth.** r = h tan C, so a source twice as deep needs a disc
twice as wide ✓ Here the convenient 3-4-5 triangle makes the arithmetic exact.
**A check on the numbers.** A ray leaving the source at exactly 36·9° to the vertical
travels 4/cos(36·9°) = **5 m** to the surface, arriving 3 m from the point directly
above ✓ consistent with the 3-4-5 triangle.
**Reading the distractors.** **4 m** ✗ uses tan C = 1, that is C = 45°, which would need
n = √2. **6 m** ✗ doubles the radius. **∞** ✗ would be right only if there were **no**
total internal reflection, that is if n = 1 ✓
∴ 3 m.
